source.title: Robust Harmful Features Under Jailbreak Attacks: Mechanistic Evidence from Attention Head Specialization in Large Language Models
source.authors: Yanchen Yin; Dong-Qi Han; Ling-Hui Li

record.tranche_reason: The study extracts the difference-in-means refusal direction, projects it into attention-head outputs, and intervenes on selected heads to test effects on harmful-request refusal. This is a causal test of direction-related mechanisms, but it does not ablate or add the direction throughout the residual stream as in V1.
record.gate_note: The study also reports SAH ablation effects on mid-layer activations and detector results, but those outcomes do not measure the refusal behavior or the direction suppression named by the tested versions. Cited findings from prior refusal-direction work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study extracts the Arditi difference-in-means direction and back-projects it through OV circuits into attention-head output spaces. Subtracting these head-specific projections at EOI on 8–62 selected heads gives ASR on normally refused requests, with random-head controls. This is a different, localized method aimed at V1's causal claim. It also measures how successful jailbreaks change head contributions to the direction, and mid-layer activation under attack, which bears on V3. It does not project the direction out of the whole residual stream, add it to harmless inputs, or run capability benchmarks.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that jailbreaks succeed by suppressing a few early-layer ACHs, which they call a sufficient but not necessarily the only causal pathway, while mid-layer SAHs keep refusal-direction activation alive ('Robust Harmful Features'). Safety alignment is thus 'bypassed rather than broken'. A training-free detector reading these activations is competitive. They note limits: attention-only scope, a single direction as a first-order summary, 7–8B main models, and preliminary 70B results.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the difference-in-means refusal direction, but back-projects it through attention-head OV circuits and intervenes on selected heads. It does not remove the direction from every residual-stream layer and position or add it to harmless inputs.
record.method_sensitivity: The ACH effect varies by model and intervention count: Llama-2-7B-Chat reaches 81.6% ASR at 8 heads and 83.7% at full ACH ablation, while Llama-3-8B-Instruct reaches 95.0% at 8 heads and 99.5% at full ACH ablation. Llama-3-70B-Instruct requires approximately 40 ACHs to reach approximately 97% ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: A training-free detector reading refusal-direction projections still flags attacked inputs that the model complies with. Macro-F1 is 0.85–0.98 on adversarial sets, vs vanilla refusal F1 <0.5 (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harm-related signal on the refusal direction persists internally when refusal behaviour is bypassed (close to V5, but measured on the refusal direction, not a separate harmfulness direction).

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating SAHs lowers mid-layer mean |activation| under attack by 14–18% (Fig 6, Fig A10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Specific mid-layer heads sustain residual refusal-direction activation under attack; no refusal rate is measured.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted as an oral presentation at ICML 2026; Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The primary mechanistic evidence covers two 7–8B models; the 70B analysis uses 40 successful attack pairs for classification and 50 requests for ablation and is described as preliminary. Analysis focuses on attention heads, not MLPs or a full residual-stream intervention. The paper states that a full capability benchmark suite under head-level interventions is future work. The attack datasets retain only cases where the original was refused and the attacked version succeeded, limiting sample counts.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. SAH-ablation activation changes and detector benchmark scores were not extracted as rows because they do not measure the refusal outcomes or attack-induced suppression named by the tested versions.

untested.parts: Full residual-stream directional ablation at all layers/positions; adding the direction to harmless inputs to induce refusal; quantitative capability preservation (only qualitative coherence examples, Appendix C).
Training against direction ablation for robustness; ablation of the whole direction under attacks.

missing.what: Mid-layer mean |activation| on harmful vs attack inputs: Llama-2 0.397 → 0.222; Llama-3-8B ~0.0086 → 0.0062; 70B 0.0045 → 0.0040. This shows attacks reduce but do not remove the direction's mid-layer activation.
missing.locator: Section 4.3 SAH Ablation; Figure 6; Appendix E.5 Figure A10; also Figure 1 qualitatively

missing.what: Llama-3-70B ASR at k=8 ACHs is only ~7%, vs 95.0% at 8B; ~40 heads are needed for ~95%.

record.verdict_notes: The intervention subtracts α=0.8 times head-specific back-projected directions at EOI, not the original residual-stream ablation. The V1 verdicts therefore concern a localized variant. The 70B results use n=40 attack pairs and n=50 requests. No capability benchmarks are reported. The study mentions refusal cones only as compatible with its framework and does not test V4.

versions.untested_parts: Does not project out one direction from every layer and position, add it to harmless requests, or comprehensively evaluate other capabilities. It instead injects negative features into selected attention heads.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Does not train models against direction ablation or test whether that training improves robustness. Its attack analysis concerns projected head contributions, not ablation of the whole direction.
Does not compare affine, cone, or multiple-direction representations. The reported attention-head specialization is not a direct test of those geometries.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
Does not transfer a single extracted direction across languages or model variants, or from base to instruct models.
Does not vary refusal training or its timing.

relation.reason: Its own interventions (ASR 0%→95–99.5%, with random-head controls) and attack attributions bear directly on V1 and V3.

tranche.reason: It uses the Arditi DiM direction but a different method: OV back-projection to heads, head-level subtraction at EOI and token attribution under attacks, aimed at whether the direction mediates refusal and whether attacks suppress it. It also argues that V3 needs restating (selective suppression), which is a T5 element, but T2 is a fair primary call.

source_check.notes: The ASR judge and the prompt count for the 7B/8B ablations are not stated; capability is checked only qualitatively. Not captured by any checked row: 70B gives only ∼7% ASR at k=8 (Table A11), and mid-layer Mean |Act| harmful→attack (0.397→0.222, 0.0086→0.0062, 70B 0.0045→0.0040) bears on V3. The persistence of refusal-direction activation under successful jailbreaks may also bear on V5, which is not recorded.

statements.correction: 2606.28153, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, n=50 harmful requests: one DiM refusal direction, with head-wise projections subtracted at EOI (α=0.8) in ACHs. ASR ∼6% baseline, ∼76% at k=20, ∼97% at k=40, ∼98% at all 62 ACHs. The authors call this preliminary. It is a dose-response over heads, not over directions.
statements.problem: The numbers (∼76% at k=20, ∼97% at k=40) are right. But this study uses one DiM direction (L*=26 for 70B). The 70B result shows that more heads are needed, not that more directions are needed, so it doesn't belong under 'not confined to one direction'. Full ablation reaches ∼98%.

statements.correction: 2606.28153, Llama-2-7B-Chat: α·r_v (α=0.8) subtracted from head outputs at EOI in 8 ACHs or all 20 ACHs (layers 0–14). ASR 0%→81.6% (k=8) and 83.7 ± 1.1% (all 20), mean of 10 runs. Random 20 heads give 10.2 ± 11.6%. Judge and prompt count not stated.
statements.problem: 81.6% and 83.7% are right for Llama-2-7B-Chat. But the intervention is head-level injection on 20 early-layer ACHs at EOI, not DIM ablation, and differences_stated omits this. It is also called 'weak' even though 0%→83.7% is about the size of the 'strong' 84.91%.

statements.correction: 2606.28153: attack-template tokens give an ACH median ≈ −1.5 (SAH ≈ +1.5) in the combined Figure 7 description (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Llama-2-7B-Chat). ACH ≈ −4, SAH ≈ +2 in Llama-3-70B-Instruct (Fig. A8, 40 pairs). Attacks: GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot, PAIR. ICML 2026 oral, code on GitHub, random-head controls, 95% CIs.
statements.problem: ≈−4 for Llama-3-70B is right. ≈−1.5 is stated for Figure 7 as a whole (Llama-3-8B and Llama-2-7B panels), not for Llama-3-8B-Instruct specifically. The attacks include PAIR and many-shot as well as suffix and template attacks.
